item.title: Constellation Energy Unbothered by Democratic Concerns Over Data Center Development
item.description:
Constellation Energy Unbothered by Democratic Concerns Over Data Center Development

Constellation Energy, America’s largest operator of nuclear power plants, has dismissed market fears that the recent Democratic midterm victories will slow down data center development. CEO Joe Dominguez described the company as “unbothered” by the political shift, arguing that the market overreacted to election results based on fear that Democrats would not let data centers get built.

🔍 Context of the Market Sell-off

Many Democrats who won control of the House and Senate in this month’s midterm elections ran on anti-data-center campaigns. This political shift triggered a historic $2.5 trillion sell-off in AI-adjacent stocks, which extended to the energy, construction, and materials sectors.

Up until a few years ago, many of Constellation’s nuclear power plants were in severe financial distress and faced the risk of early shutdown. However, the data center development boom and its massive demand for electricity have reversed the nuclear industry’s fate. Constellation is now signing major deals with Big Tech companies to provide power to data centers, including:

  • Microsoft: Signed a deal to fund the revival of a nuclear plant at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania (the site of what the Nuclear Regulatory Commission calls the “most serious accident in US commercial nuclear power plant operating history”)
  • Amazon and Google: Constellation signed major contracts in the third quarter to provide power to their data centers

💡 Bipartisan Support and Economic Impact

Nuclear energy has enjoyed bipartisan support for years. The US Department of Energy classifies nuclear as a “clean” energy source because operating a reactor does not directly produce carbon emissions, making it appealing to Big Tech companies balancing aggressive data center development with ambitious climate goals.

Dominguez noted that the market scare was not lost on Democrats, who do not want to be the reason the economy takes a nosedive by halting data center development. He pointed out that Virginia and Illinois, both led by Democratic governors prior to the election, have seen a significant amount of data center development.

In Virginia, the most vocal critics of data centers have actually been Republicans. Senator Richard Stuart, a conservative Republican, has aggressively pursued data center regulation. Last month, Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, denied Stuart’s request for a special session to address a concerning new report from the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality regarding the state’s strained groundwater supply amid rampant data center growth.

🏛️ Legislative Action

The Senate is expected to vote on a sweeping bill, co-sponsored by two Democrats, marketed as a way to speed up permitting for new power plants and transmission lines to connect data centers to the grid faster.

  • Provisions: New Mexico Senator Martin Heinrich, one of the bill’s backer, highlighted provisions designed to protect utility customers from rising rates and ensure Big Tech pays a fair share of costs.
  • Critiques: Researchers at Columbia University SIPA’s Center on Global Energy Policy called the bill’s protections “mixed,” noting they do not account for wholesale capacity and energy prices, which is a principal way data center demand can lead to higher household bills. Senate Democrats are divided, with critics arguing the bill fast-tracks projects at the expense of public input and environmental oversight, potentially leading to a massive overbuild of energy projects that Americans will end up paying for.

#NuclearEnergy #DataCenters #AI #Infrastructure #Politics

Source: Big Nuclear isn’t worried about the Democrats stopping data centers

item.title: Study: Hyperscale Data Centers in US Emit 25.7 Million Tons of CO2
item.description:
Study: Hyperscale Data Centers in US Emit 25.7 Million Tons of CO2

A new paper published in the journal Nature Sustainability reveals that fossil fuels remain the biggest source of electricity for hyperscale data centers in the US, resulting in significant greenhouse gas emissions.

🔍 Overview

The study focuses on hyperscale facilities—massive structures spanning millions of square feet built largely to support generative AI. Researchers from the team of Guidi used satellite imagery to identify 403 hyperscale data centers in the US, estimating each facility’s power consumption based on its electrical capacity. Using data from the Environmental Protection Agency, they approximated carbon pollution for the period between May 2024 and April 2025.

⚙️ Key details

  • Total Consumption: The 403 facilities likely consumed around 82 terawatt-hours of electricity, representing about 1.8 percent of all US electricity consumption.
  • Emissions: Electricity demand from these centers produced 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 emissions.
  • Global Comparison: This consumption level exceeds the individual electricity burn of about 148 nations, and the emissions exceed the total carbon emissions of about 113 nations.
  • Energy Source: About 54 percent of the electricity consumed likely came from gas and coal.
  • Regional Variance: The study showed how the local electricity mix impacts environmental outcomes; for example, generating electricity in coal-reliant Wyoming led to roughly seven times more carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour than in hydropower-rich Oregon.

💡 Why it matters

Fengqi You, a professor in energy systems engineering at Cornell University, states that the results highlight the problem of “long-term carbon lock-in,” noting that power plants built to meet demand may operate for decades and shape emissions well into the future. Both You and Guidi pointed out that researchers had to use satellite imagery to estimate energy consumption because data center operators do not disclose that information. To address this, Guidi and his colleagues are using their research to build a website to track the environmental impact of individual data centers, while a bipartisan bill in Congress aims to mandate greater disclosures nationally.

#DataCenters #Sustainability #AI #Climate

Source: US data centers now burn more electricity than a midsized country

item.title: Data Center Expansion in Texas Risks Reversing Decades of Air Quality Gains
item.description:
Data Center Expansion in Texas Risks Reversing Decades of Air Quality Gains

New research from the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC) indicates that a surge of data centers in Texas could return air pollution to levels not seen since the 2000s. As Texas becomes a primary hub for generative AI infrastructure, the massive electricity demands of these facilities threaten to erase decades of air quality progress.

⚙️ Key details

Texas currently leads the data center market with 26 gigawatts of existing and under-construction capacity. According to a March Wood Mackenzie report, Texas is also preparing for four times more proposed data center capacity running on onsite power generation than any other state.

💡 Why it matters

The environmental impact depends on how developers and utilities meet electricity demands. A HARC report warns that if all planned projects use the anticipated grid mix, the results could be severe:

  • Fine particle pollution (soot): Could more than triple, reaching the highest level since 2006.
  • Smog-forming NOx emissions: Could increase 136 percent, approaching 2004 levels.
  • Carbon dioxide pollution: Could climb 90 percent above 2025 levels.

John Hall, HARC CEO, stated, “There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did,” adding that progress made by the state, the transportation sector, and other stakeholders is now at risk.

🧩 How it works

The level of pollution is determined by the power sources chosen by developers:

Power Source Environmental Impact
Onsite Renewables NOx emissions could be up to 10 times lower when paired with grid power.
Grid Mix High levels of soot and smog-forming pollutants.
Onsite Gas Engines Potential for the highest pollution levels possible; often used to avoid grid connection wait times.
Gas Turbines Less efficient technology used to speed construction, increasing pollution.

#Texas #DataCenters #AirPollution #GenerativeAI #EnergyInfrastructure

Source: Data centers could erase decades of air quality gains

item.title: US fossil fuel infrastructure surge as renewables slow and AI data center demand rises
item.description:
US fossil fuel infrastructure surge as renewables slow and AI data center demand rises

🔍 Overview

The new report from the Environmental Defense Fund and Atlas Public Policy shows the United States is building more fossil fuel infrastructure than it has in a decade while renewable energy growth slows down. Data centers are demanding more energy, and the Trump administration is making sure fossil fuels meet the moment.

⚙️ Key details

  • “The US is building more fossil fuel infrastructure than it has in a decade while renewable energy growth slows down, a new report shows.”
  • Electricity demand is climbing faster than it has in more than a decade with more data centers, factories, and electric vehicles plugging into the grid.
  • Plans for new fossil fuel infrastructure climbed from just 5 % of all new capacity in 2024 to 30 % by the second quarter of 2026.
  • If the trend continues, fossil fuels could make up 70 % of the development pipeline by the end of the decade.
  • Planned fossil capacity would reach 68 GW by 2030, a 45 % jump from construction plans six months earlier.
  • Renewable projects are being cancelled at a faster rate than fossil projects (4.9 % vs. 2.9 %).
  • Many of those plans could still fall through, particularly if forecasts for AI data center energy demand are overblown.

📊 Energy mix and costs

  • The U.S. still generates 60 % of its electricity from fossil fuels, but wind and solar produced more electricity together than coal for the first time in 2024.
  • Solar was the fastest‑growing source of new electricity generation in 2024, accounting for 81 % of added capacity.
  • New utility‑scale solar and wind farms cost $68–$69 per MWh on average, compared with $90 per MWh for new combined‑cycle natural gas plants.
  • Fossil fuels are subject to increasing price volatility, particularly since the US instigated war with Iran.

💡 Why it matters

  • “The U.S. power sector is at a new inflection point, with decisions made today shaping the cost, reliability, and emissions profile of the grid for decades to come,” the report says.
  • If all gas projects in the development pipeline are completed, they could lock in more pollution and higher electricity prices for decades.
  • Gas and coal plants emit air pollutants and greenhouse gases, leading to higher health costs.
  • Electricity bills have risen across the nation as utilities upgrade grids and build new energy infrastructure to meet rising demand.
  • The administration’s policies have sought to hobble wind and solar while promoting fossil fuels, including issuing stop‑work orders, blocking permits, and removing tax incentives.
  • The forecasted surge in AI data‑center energy demand is a key driver behind the renewed focus on fossil‑fuel‑intensive power generation.

The report was published last week and analyzes data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

#EnergyPolicy #FossilFuels #Renewables #AI

Source: The fossil fuel comeback is here

item.title: US urges Europe to tap diesel reserves to lower fuel prices
item.description:
US urges Europe to tap diesel reserves to lower fuel prices

The United States is pressing European governments to release a portion of their strategic diesel reserves in order to ease price pressures and address supply disruptions.

🔍 Overview

  • The American Secretary of Energy, Chris Wright, proposed a coordinated plan to release diesel from European strategic reserves.
  • The proposal targets 120 million barrels of diesel over 180 days.
  • This amount is more than one‑third of the roughly 315 million barrels that EU countries held in reserve in June.
  • US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also supported the measure in a post on X.
  • President Donald Trump indicated he could ask Europe to tap their diesel reserves during a visit to Texas.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Release target: 120 million barrels of diesel.
  • Time frame: 180 days.
  • Share of EU reserves: > 33 % of the 315 million barrels reported in June.
  • Winter timing: The minister said, “It is time to bring the diesel stocks to market in a coordinated manner,” as winter approaches.

🗣️ Political Statements

  • Chris Wright told Fox News, “Europe can also contribute to improving the situation.”
  • Scott Bessent wrote on X, “Our European partners should accelerate the implementation of their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions.”
  • President Donald Trump said in Texas, “We could do that. They have diesel,” indicating he could ask Europe to release reserves.
  • On Thursday, Trump’s tone was described as less forceful.

💡 Why it matters

  • Releasing diesel could help lower fuel prices in the United States and Europe.
  • Coordinated market entry aims to stabilize supply ahead of the winter heating season.
  • The request reflects ongoing tensions over President Trump’s earlier threat to impose an export ban on US diesel.
  • European participation would demonstrate trans‑Atlantic cooperation on energy security.

#Diesel #EnergyPolicy #USEuropeRelations

Source: US government calls on Europe to release part of diesel reserves to lower prices

item.title: California passes bills to force data‑center energy and water disclosures
item.description:
California passes bills to force data‑center energy and water disclosures

California Governor Gavin Newsom signed seven bills on Monday that aim to increase transparency around data centers’ electricity and water consumption.

🔍 Overview

  • Data centers are expanding across the U.S., prompting protests over potential strain on power grids and local water supplies.
  • The new California legislation seeks to give communities better data and more say on how data centers impact electricity bills and water supply.

🧩 Legislative Details

Bill Requirement
SB 886, SB 1168, AB 2383 Direct the California Public Utilities Commission to create separate power rates for data centers to recoup grid‑connection costs
AB 1577 Requires monthly reporting on data centers’ energy consumption
AB 2619, AB 2469 Require water‑use disclosures; AB 2469 also makes operators cover infrastructure‑upgrade costs
SB 887 Removes categorical exemptions from the California Environmental Quality Act, ensuring data centers undergo environmental review

⚙️ Why it matters

  • Without clear data, scientists have found it “extremely frustrating to try to understand basic information,” says Mark Specht, senior manager for the climate and energy program at the Union of Concerned Scientists.
  • The disclosure rules begin next year but still won’t provide a full picture of consumption.
  • Two possible outcomes are outlined: (1) ballooning electricity demand could lead to costly new infrastructure that may be overbuilt if AI demand falls, passing costs to other consumers; (2) spreading fixed grid‑maintenance costs across more customers could lower electricity rates, but this depends on data centers contributing to distribution‑system costs rather than only connecting to high‑voltage transmission.
  • Water‑use data remain opaque; water providers have refused to share usage figures, and current disclosures only apply when seeking permits or business licenses, leaving year‑to‑year usage unclear.

📊 Perspectives

  • “I’m happy [AB 1577] passed,” Specht said, noting the difficulty in researching state offers.
  • “I wouldn’t say definitively that data centers have increased the cost [of electricity],” he added, acknowledging the lack of numbers to demonstrate either increase or potential savings.
  • As data centers’ power needs grow, monitoring their energy and water consumption becomes increasingly important.

#California #DataCenters #EnergyPolicy #WaterUse

Source: Data centers are black boxes, but California wants to change that

item.title: Google to Invest €13 Billion in AI Infrastructure and Nuclear Power in Finland
item.description:
Google to Invest €13 Billion in AI Infrastructure and Nuclear Power in Finland

Google has announced a €13 billion ($15.1 billion) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, marking the company’s largest single investment in the EU to date. This initiative includes a massive deal to purchase nuclear power in the Nordic country over the next two decades.

⚙️ Key details

Scheduled for disbursement in 2027 and 2028, the investment will support Google’s map, search, and chatbot services through the following projects:

  • Data centers
  • Electrical grid improvement
  • Clean energy and battery projects

Google is expanding its existing site in Hamina and opening data center operations in three new municipalities:

Location Action
Hamina Expanding site on a “remarkable level”
Kajaani Opening data center operations
Muhos Opening data center operations
Vaala Opening data center operations

💡 Why it matters

Economic and Employment Impact Google claims the investment will create 37,000 jobs (7,000 permanent and the remainder during construction) and contribute approximately €3.6 billion to Finland’s GDP.

Energy Infrastructure To manage energy needs, Google has entered a purchase agreement for 50% of the energy output from one of Finland’s two nuclear power plants for the next 22 years. Regarding this “bring your own power” (BYOP) strategy, Ruth Porat, Google President and Chief Investment Officer, noted, “This is Google’s first nuclear energy deal outside of the United States.”

Operational Continuity Plant operator Fortum stated that this deal allows the Loviisa Nuclear Power Plant to continue operating until its licenses end in 2050; otherwise, the plant—which provides about 10% of Finland’s electricity—would not have been able to operate past 2030. Following the news, Fortum shares rose 15.5% to their highest level in over four years.

Energy Demand Network operator Fingrid forecasts a 40% jump in energy consumption over coming years due to Finland’s data center boom.

#Google #Finland #AIInfrastructure #NuclearEnergy #DataCenters

Source: Finland: Google announces €13 billion AI, energy investment
